input.question: Sometimes I feel tired or discouraged—how can I stay motivated, [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE]
input.story:
Every morning, I wake up before sunrise in my small village outside [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE], ready to open my trading stall at the market. Sometimes I skip breakfast because I want to hurry and set up my small table. I pack some fried dough and sweet tea to nibble on, thinking it will give me energy for the day. But, ah, last week I tried carrying a bag of onions to my stall and suddenly felt tired—the bag almost slipped from my hands! I sat down, sweating and a bit dizzy. Chai, is it because I didn’t eat well, or maybe my sugar is doing its wahala again? Work feels harder when my body is not right.

On market day, a [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] health worker from our local clinic, Aunty Hadiza, stopped at my stall. She asked me about my insulin and how I am feeling these days. I told her, 'Sometimes I just feel weak, wallahi.' She smiled, sat beside me, and said, 'Participant, eating small healthy snacks and doing some simple moving, like stretching your legs, can help your sugar and make you strong for trading. Why not try roasted groundnuts or cucumber instead of fried foods?' Me, I was not so sure—it sounded odd. Won’t too many snacks make my sugar high? But she said, 'Just a handful, and walk around your stall if you feel sleepy. You will see gradually.'

I tried her advice the next day. During the slow afternoon, I reached for my roasted groundnuts and chewed slowly, instead of my usual sweet tea. It felt strange, almost like I was missing something. Later, when I started packing up my goods, my legs felt tired, so I walked slowly around the small market for a bit before going home, but it was not easy. Habits are hard to change, isn’t it? But I remembered the big market festival coming soon, where I must help my mother and sisters with a bigger load than usual. I said to myself, let me try small, small each day.

Days passed, and I kept up with my new routine—a handful of groundnuts, a little walk, sometimes adding sliced cucumber when I could find. When the festival day came, I woke up strong and helped my family set up our biggest market stall yet. This time, I carried onions and yams without feeling tired so quickly. I even joked with my [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE], laughing as we worked together. I thanked Allah for making my body better, and now, I am not afraid to learn new ways to care for myself, wallahi. If I can do it once, maybe I can keep getting better, one market day at a time.

input.question: Eating healthy can get expensive—how can I manage a nutritious diet on a tight budget? And can I still enjoy some traditional foods?
input.story:
One week, I tried to get my goods ready for the big Sallah sale, but as I stood over my stall, my legs felt weak, and my head spun a little. Was it the hot sun, or the leftover fried masa I had gobbled in a rush? I missed a few sales because I had to sit down and recover. I wondered, can I really do well at my work if I keep eating like this? The answer came sharply that day: I lost a customer, and spent the rest of the day worrying. Food can make or break a [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] like me.

A day later, at the clinic, I met Sister Habiba, our nurse. She saw worry on my face and asked, 'Participant, are you eating well before market?' I hesitated and told her my challenge. Instead of scolding, she gave practical advice: 'You don’t need rich people’s food for good health. Boil your tuwo shinkafa or millet instead of frying. Add beans, groundnut, little vegetables from your farm, and use less oil. You can still enjoy Hausa dishes, my dear—just prepare them in a way that keeps your sugar happy and your pocket safe.' That sounded simple, but could I really do it?

The next week, I tried boiling my tuwo and grilling my fish instead of frying. It felt odd and the smell was new. Old habit wanted me to pour palm oil over everything, but I remembered Sister Habiba’s words. The first time, my brothers made faces at the plain food, and even I wanted to put the oil back! Still, I kept on—thinking of Eid market, the big work task ahead. It was only food, and yet, wasn’t this small change for my own future?

Little by little, I noticed my mornings grew steadier. No more dizzy legs as I set out my goods. On Eid, I helped with the bigger trade without feeling tired. I smiled more, and my family saw me shine. Maybe healthy eating isn’t for the rich—maybe it’s for smart Hausa women like me, who love our food and want to live well. With these small changes, I can keep trading, farming, and enjoying life while caring for my health, one careful meal at a time.

input.question: [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE]
input.story:
I am Participant, a Hausa woman from [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE]. I work every day as a [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] in the market, and I go to the same place every morning. I buy things like beans, millet, and fish. I cook with what I find. I know I have diabetes, and I take insulin every day. But I don’t always think about how my food and how I move affect my body. I used to think eating a big meal would make me strong, but now I see it makes me tired. I don’t know how to mix food with my work or how to move without hurting my body. I just do what I know. That’s how I live.

One day, I went to the clinic near my home. A kind nurse told me, 'Participant, your blood sugar is high, and you need to eat better and move more. You don’t need to stop working, but you can change how you eat and walk.' She said, 'Try small meals with vegetables and beans. And walk after your work, even just for ten minutes.' I said, 'But I don’t have time!' She smiled and said, 'You do. Just walk after you finish your work. It’s not much, but it helps your body feel better.' I didn’t say yes right away. I was scared it would take me away from my trade. But I remembered I have a big task coming — I need to open my own small shop soon, and I want to be strong for that.

I tried walking after work. At first, I didn’t like it. My legs felt heavy. I used to walk to the market with my cart, and now I had to stop. I thought, 'Why can’t I just go straight to my stall?' One day, I forgot to walk, and I felt dizzy. My hands shook. I knew I had made a mistake. I went back to the clinic and asked the nurse again. She said, 'You just need to start small. Walk with your cart, just five minutes. Then you’ll get used to it.' I did it again. I walked slowly with my cart, and I felt better. I told myself, 'If I can do this, I can open my shop and be strong for my family.' That kept me going.

Now, every day after work, I walk with my cart for ten minutes. I eat millet with spinach and a little fish. I don’t eat too much sugar. I feel more energy, and my hands don’t shake as much. I even shared my story with a few women in the market. They said, 'Participant, you are helping us too!' I feel proud. I know I can keep going. I will keep walking, keep eating well, and one day I will open my own shop — not just with money, but with health and strength. I am not just a [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE]. I am a woman who is learning to care for herself.

input.question: I like to snack—what are some healthy options and how often should I have them?
input.story:
I'm Participant, a 58-year-old man from [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE], and I run my own small business selling traditional Hausa goods. I wake up early, go to work, and come home to pray. I know I have diabetes and high blood pressure, but I don’t really think about how my snacks affect my work or my energy. I just eat what’s around — like roasted groundnuts or sweet dates — when I feel hungry. I don’t check my blood sugar, and I don’t plan snacks. I think, 'If I eat now, I’ll feel strong for the day.' But I don’t know that sugar spikes can make me tired or dizzy later. I just follow what I’ve always done.

One morning, I had a meeting with a health worker at the clinic. She said, 'You need to eat small, healthy snacks every 3 to 4 hours, not just when you’re hungry.' I said, 'But I don’t have time. I’m busy with my shop and prayers.' She smiled and said, 'Try a handful of roasted groundnuts or a slice of unripe plantain. No sugar, no milk. Just good, simple food.' I thought, 'Maybe I can do this.' But I didn’t believe it would help. I tried it once — after my prayer, I ate a few groundnuts — and I felt okay. But the next day, I forgot. I ate a whole date, and I felt dizzy. I told the health worker, 'I don’t know how to do this right.' She said, 'Just start small. One snack a day. You’ll get used to it.'

I tried again, but I messed up. I had a big meeting at the shop, and I got so busy I skipped my snack. After that, I felt weak and my hands shook. I didn’t want to go to the clinic again. But then I heard that the city is hosting a big Islamic business fair in two weeks — I have to present my goods and talk to other entrepreneurs. I said to myself, 'If I don’t feel strong, I won’t be able to speak clearly or answer questions.' So I started again. I took a small handful of roasted groundnuts before work, and I ate a piece of unripe plantain after my prayer. It wasn’t easy — I had to stop eating sweet things. But I kept doing it. I felt better, and I didn’t get dizzy.

Now, I eat a small, healthy snack every 3 to 4 hours. I don’t skip meals. I use roasted groundnuts, unripe plantain, or a few slices of banana. I check my blood sugar once a week and talk to the health worker. I even brought a small tin of roasted groundnuts to the business fair. When I spoke, I felt strong. The people listened. I didn’t feel dizzy. I felt proud. I told my friends, 'This is how I manage my health now.' I know I can do more — maybe add more vegetables or try baobab tea. But today, I feel confident. I know my body is strong, and I know I can keep going.

input.question: Sometimes I feel tired or discouraged—how can I stay motivated, [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE]
input.story:
I wake up early like every day, before the sun even shows. I go to my shop near the market, and I sell dried fish and plantain. My body feels heavy, like it’s carrying all the work. I don’t think much about my blood sugar — I just eat what’s on hand. I eat late at night because I have to finish my work. But why do I feel tired? Why can’t I move when I go to the shop? I don’t know. I just do it. I tell myself, ‘One more day, then I’ll rest.’ But the next day, I feel worse. I don’t even want to walk to the market. I just sit and watch the sun go down. What if I could feel strong again? What if I could walk without my legs shaking? I don’t know how to fix it, but I know I need to try something new.

Last month, I went to the health clinic. I told the nurse about my tiredness. She listened, and then she said, ‘Participant, your blood sugar is high, and your blood pressure is also high. That’s why you feel tired. You need to eat better and move your body.’ I said, ‘But I don’t have time. I have to sell fish every day.’ She smiled and said, ‘You don’t need to stop selling. You just need to eat small meals, like before the sun rises. And you can walk with your basket to the market — just 10 minutes a day. It helps your blood sugar go down.’ I said, ‘Can I do that?’ She said, ‘Yes. And you can start tomorrow.’ I didn’t believe it at first. But I thought — if I can walk just 10 minutes, maybe I can feel better. Maybe I can do more for my family.

I tried walking with my basket. But on the first day, I was so tired. I didn’t even make it to the market. I sat under the tree near the mosque and cried. I said to myself, ‘I can’t do this. I am not strong like before.’ My husband said, ‘Participant, you don’t have to be strong all the time. Just walk a little. You will feel better.’ I tried again the next day. I walked to the market and back. I didn’t eat much, just a small bowl of rice and a little salad. I felt weak, but I didn’t stop. I told myself, ‘I have a big task coming — I have to grow a small garden for my family. If I can grow vegetables, I can feed them with [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] food. That means I need to be healthy.’ So I kept walking. I kept eating small meals. I didn’t feel strong, but I felt like I was trying.

Now, I walk every morning. I walk with my basket, and I carry a small pot of water. I eat a small meal before I go to the market. I feel better. My blood sugar is not as high. I don’t feel tired when I go to work. I even talk to my neighbours and say, ‘Participant walked today. She feels strong.’ I still have a big task — to grow a garden. But now I know I can do it. I know that walking helps my body. I know that small changes make a big difference. I don’t need to be perfect. I just need to keep trying. And every day, I feel a little stronger. Maybe one day, I will grow enough vegetables to feed my whole family. And I will be proud of how I took care of my body.

I used to think that being tired was just part of life. Now I know it’s not. My body is like a car — if you don’t take care of it, it breaks down. But if you drive it gently, it lasts longer. I don’t have to stop working. I just need to move a little. I don’t need to eat big meals. I just need to eat small, healthy food. And I don’t need to walk far — just 10 minutes a day. I am not a doctor, but I am learning. I am learning to listen to my body. And every time I walk, I feel a little more like myself. I feel like I can do more. I feel like I can grow. I feel like I can help my family. And that makes me happy.

input.question: [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE]
input.story:
I’m Participant, a [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] who works the land every morning before the sun is high. I used to eat late at night — after work, when the day is done and the farm is quiet. I’d eat a piece of bread with a bit of meat, just to feel full. I never thought it would matter. 'What’s the harm?' I’d say to myself. 'I’m not sick, I’m just tired.' But then I started feeling dizzy at night, like my head was spinning. My hands would shake when I tried to pick up a bucket. I didn’t know then that eating late at night could make my blood sugar go up and down. I just thought it was the heat or the work. I didn’t know what insulin was for — I only knew it was something I had to take. So I kept eating late, and my body started to complain. And now, I’m wondering — if I stop eating late, will I still be strong enough to work the farm tomorrow? Or will I fall down like I did last week?

One day, I went to the clinic near the market. The nurse, Mrs. Nandi, was kind and said, 'Participant, you’re not eating right. Your blood sugar goes high at night, and that makes your body weak. You need to eat small meals during the day and stop eating after 7 p.m.' I said, 'But I’m a [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE]. I work hard. I need energy.' She smiled and said, 'Yes, but your body needs balance. If you eat too much at night, your body can’t use the sugar properly. You’ll feel tired and weak.' I didn’t believe her at first. I thought, 'I’ve been doing this for years.' But she gave me a simple plan — eat a banana with a spoon of milk before bed, not bread or meat. And I agreed. I said, 'Okay, I’ll try it. But I don’t want to lose strength.' She said, 'You won’t. You’ll just be stronger in the morning.'

I tried the banana and milk at first. I thought, 'This is too soft. I need something heavy.' So I ate a piece of bread with it, just to feel full. The next day, I felt dizzy again. I fell off the ladder while watering the plants. I was shaking. I knew I’d made a mistake. I didn’t want to fail. But then I remembered — next week, I have to help my cousin build a new fence on the farm. It’s a big job. I can’t fall and break a leg before that. So I told myself: 'I’ll do it again. I’ll eat only the banana and milk. No bread. No meat. Just what the nurse said.' I tried it again. And this time, I felt better. Not perfect, but better.

After a week, I noticed a change. I didn’t feel dizzy at night. My hands didn’t shake. I woke up feeling strong. I could walk the farm without stopping. I even helped my cousin with the fence. We built it in two days — faster than usual. When I saw the fence, I smiled. I said, 'This is what happens when you listen to your body.' I didn’t think I’d ever feel this good. Now, I tell my friends — 'Don’t eat late at night. Your body will thank you.' I still take my insulin every day, but now I feel like I’m in control. I know what I need. And I know that small changes can make a big difference. I’m not just a [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE]. I’m a man who listens to his body. And that’s how I stay strong.

input.question: Sometimes I feel tired or discouraged—how can I stay motivated, [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE]
input.story:
Every morning, Participant wakes up and makes a small breakfast. She has a banana and a glass of milk. She thinks, 'This is enough. I’m not hungry.' But after eating, she feels heavy. Her legs feel like they’re made of sand. She walks to her little garden, where she plants herbs. She picks a few thyme leaves and puts them in a bowl. She smiles and says, 'I’m doing good.' But by afternoon, she feels weak. She sits on the back step and just watches the birds. She thinks, 'Why can’t I just stay still?' Then she remembers—her health worker said, 'Walking helps your blood sugar go down. Even a little walk helps.' She didn’t believe it at first. 'I’m not strong enough,' she said. But the health worker just smiled and said, 'Try it. Just five minutes. No pressure.' And that’s when she decided to try.

So Participant walks. First, she walks to the corner shop to buy a loaf of bread. She walks slowly, her feet touching the ground like a slow dance. She feels her legs move, and she thinks, 'This is new.' But after two days, she forgets. She eats a chocolate bar and sits down. She feels worse. Her hands shake. She says, 'I can’t do this.' But then she remembers: next week, she has to teach a new group. She has to speak clearly. She can’t be tired. So she tries again. This time, she walks to the park. She walks with her shoes on, her arms swinging. The sun is warm on her skin. She feels the breeze. She says to herself, 'I can do this. Just for the lesson.' She doesn’t run. She doesn’t race. She just walks. And slowly, she feels better.

After a week, Participant walks every day. She walks after her lesson, before she eats. She walks to the neighbour’s house to say hello. She walks past the old tree where the children play. She feels strong. Her legs don’t feel heavy. Her blood sugar feels balanced. She doesn’t need sugar or sweets to feel happy. She says to her friend, 'I didn’t think walking would help so much.' And the friend says, 'Maybe it does.' Participant smiles. She knows now that small things matter. She has a new habit. And when she teaches her lesson, she speaks with confidence. The group says, 'You are so calm and strong.' She feels proud. She knows she can keep going. And she knows—walking is not just for the body. It’s for the heart too. And maybe, one day, she’ll teach a lesson about movement, too.

Participant walks every day now. She walks with her hands in her pockets, her head up. She doesn’t rush. She watches the birds. She listens to the wind. She knows her body is learning. She knows that small steps can change everything. And when she feels tired, she doesn’t stop. She just walks a little more. She knows that her diabetes is not a problem. It’s a part of her life. And with care, it can be managed. She says to herself, 'I can do this. I am strong. I am healthy. I am Participant.' And she smiles. And she walks.

input.question: I like to snack—what are some healthy options and how often should I have them?
input.story:
My name is Participant, and I’m a [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] here in Dutse. It’s a tough job, always on the road, picking up passengers and trying to make enough to get by. Most days, I start with a big plate of Tuwo Shinkafa – that’s like a really thick rice pudding – and some fried plantains. It’s filling, and it keeps me going until lunchtime. Honestly, I don’t really think about anything else. I grab some roasted corn from the roadside vendors, maybe a few biscuits if I’m feeling fancy, and that’s usually it. My work keeps me busy, and I just… eat when I’m hungry. It’s simple, it’s easy, and it’s what I’m used to. I don't really have time to think about things like ‘healthy’ or ‘diabetes’ – I just need to get to the next pickup.

Yesterday, I had a really important trip – I was supposed to take a group of students to a school outside of town. I was running late, and I’d grabbed a quick plate of Tuwo Shinkafa and some moi moi from a vendor near the station. But halfway through the journey, I started feeling really shaky and dizzy. My head was spinning, and I couldn’t even focus on the road. I pulled over, completely panicked. The students were worried, and I felt terrible. That’s when I realized something was seriously wrong. I'd never really felt like this before, and it was scary. I knew I needed help, so I called the clinic in town, and a nurse came to check me out. She said my blood sugar was dangerously low, and I needed to eat something immediately.

The nurse, Participant, was really kind. She explained that my diet – all that rice and fried food – was probably the problem. She told me about the importance of eating smaller, more frequent meals and choosing foods that wouldn’t spike my blood sugar. She gave me a little card with some pictures of healthy options – things like boiled beans, fruits, and some vegetables. I tried to follow her advice, but it was hard. I’m used to eating big meals, and changing my habits felt overwhelming. I tried to eat a handful of roasted peanuts for a snack, but I kept craving that Tuwo Shinkafa. It was frustrating, and I almost gave up. I was worried about missing my next trip, and honestly, I just didn't know how to do it.

But then I remembered the big trip I was supposed to take – a field trip for the students. I knew I needed to be strong and focused for that. So, I kept trying. I started taking a small bag of boiled beans with me on my trips, and I made sure to drink water instead of sugary drinks. It wasn’t easy, and I still slipped up sometimes, but slowly, I started to feel better. The dizziness went away, and I felt more energetic. I even managed to make it through that field trip without any problems. It wasn’t perfect, but I was proud of myself for taking care of my health. Now, I'm thinking about making small changes, one step at a time, and I realize that taking care of myself is important, even if it’s just a little bit at a time.

input.question: I don't have a gym—what can I do at home or with everyday items to stay active?
input.story:
My name is Participant, and I live out here near [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] town. Life is good, mostly. My work is farming – helping my father with the millet and maize. We wake up before the sun, and it’s hard work, always. Breakfast is usually just a bit of koko – that’s groundnut milk – and maybe some bread if we’re lucky. Lunch is often just rice and stew, maybe with some vegetables if we can find them. Sometimes, if we have a good harvest, we’ll have some meat, but mostly it’s just staples. I don’t really think about how healthy it is, you know? It’s just what we eat. Yesterday, I was helping my father repair the irrigation channel – a long, hard job, digging and moving rocks. I was feeling okay at first, but then my legs started to ache, and I felt really tired. I didn't stop to rest, just kept going, wanting to finish the job quickly. It was a mistake, I know. 

Later that afternoon, my father took me to the clinic in town. Dr. Participant, he’s a good man, listened to my chest and checked my blood sugar. He said I was a bit low, and that my legs were hurting because I hadn’t rested enough. He explained that if I keep pushing myself without taking care of my body, it will only get worse. He showed me pictures of my heart and blood vessels, and how diabetes can damage them. It was a little scary, but he told me it wasn't too late to change things. He said I need to eat more vegetables and fruits, and that I should take short breaks while I’m working, even just a few minutes to sit down and catch my breath. He gave me a simple plan – a few minutes of walking each day, and to make sure I drink plenty of water. It seemed like a lot, but he said it was important to start small.

I tried to follow his advice, I really did. I started walking for ten minutes after lunch, but then my younger brother needed help with his schoolwork, and I just ended up helping him instead. And then my mother asked me to fetch water from the well, and I felt too tired to stop. It’s hard to change habits, you know? We always work, always working.  Yesterday, I tripped over a rock while carrying a bucket of water, and I twisted my ankle a little. It hurt, and I felt frustrated. It felt like I was making things worse, not better. I almost gave up on the walking, thinking it wasn't worth the effort. But then I remembered my father saying I needed to be strong for the harvest – we have to repair the fence before the rains come, and that’s a big job.

Today, I walked for twenty minutes after lunch, and I felt…better. Not perfect, but better. My ankle still aches a little, but it’s not as bad. I even helped my father fix the fence – I was careful to take breaks and drink plenty of water. It wasn't easy, but I finished it, and it felt good. I realize now that taking care of myself isn’t just about avoiding sickness; it’s about being able to do the things I need to do, like helping my family and farming our land. Dr. Participant was right. Small steps, every day, can make a big difference. Maybe tomorrow, I'll try to eat a little more of the okra my mother grows – it looks good and healthy.  It’s a start, and that’s enough for now.

input.story:
My name is Participant, and I sell grains here in [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE]. It’s a good job, keeps a roof over my head and food on the table. Most days, I start early, sorting millet and rice, making sure it’s good for the market. I eat a lot of rice, you know? Just a big plate, every meal. Sometimes, I’ll throw in some beans, if I have the money. My wife, Participant, she makes sure we have some vegetables, but honestly, sometimes it’s just too much rice. I don't really think about my blood sugar much, to be honest. My uncle told me about it once, but it felt like a long time ago.  Do I really need to worry about that when I’m just trying to work and provide for my family?

Yesterday, I was helping my brother, Musa, load a truck with sacks of sorghum. It was a hot day, and we were moving fast. I was sweating, and I felt a bit dizzy, but I just pushed through. I thought, ‘Participant, you need to be strong for Musa.’ But halfway through, my legs just felt weak, and I almost dropped a sack. Musa shouted at me, saying I was being careless. I felt embarrassed, and my head started to spin worse. It was a proper mess, and we had to stop for a bit. I just grabbed a cold bottle of Zobo and tried to think about something else. I was worried, not about the sacks, but about feeling like this again.

Dr. Participant at the clinic explained things to me. He said my body was telling me something – that the rice and beans weren’t agreeing with my blood sugar. He showed me a picture of a sugar test, and he said it was important to check it regularly. He told me to eat smaller portions of rice, and to add more vegetables and fruits to my meals. He even suggested some Hausa dishes like Tuwo Shinkafa with a bit of okra – that sounds good, doesn’t it? He said a little bit of sweetness from the fruits and vegetables would help.  It felt a bit strange, changing things I’d done for so long, but he said it was for my health, and for Musa too.  I promised to try, really try.

It hasn’t been easy

input.question: Sometimes I feel tired or discouraged—how can I stay motivated, [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE]
input.story:
My name is Participant, and I sell fruit and veggies at the market down by the station. It's a busy place, always full of people shouting and laughing. I usually start work before the sun even thinks about waking up, you know? I grab a quick piece of pap and some beans – that’s my breakfast. It keeps me going, I tell you. Sometimes I feel tired, like my legs are heavy, but I push on. I need to make enough money to pay the rent, and buy insulin for my blood pressure. It's a tough job, lugging crates and shouting prices.  Do you ever just feel like you can’t keep going?

Yesterday, I had to pack a big order for Mr. Maphalane, the [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE]. He wanted a mountain of mangoes and pineapples. I was rushing, trying to get everything done quickly, and I forgot to take a proper break. I was so focused on getting the order right, I didn't even drink some water.  I tripped over a crate of oranges and spilled half the mangoes! Mr. Maphalane wasn’t happy, and I felt terrible. It made me realise I’m not thinking about myself at all. I need to slow down, I think. My blood pressure is always worrying me, and I need to look after my body, you know?

Today, I went to see Dr. Sithole at the clinic. He’s a good man, always explaining things in a way you can understand. He told me that exercise helps with my blood pressure, and that eating healthy food – not just pap and beans all the time – can make a big difference. He said even a short walk each day can help. He also said that when I feel tired, it’s important to rest and drink plenty of water. He gave me a little booklet with some simple recipes. It felt a bit strange, talking about my health like that, but he seemed to really care.  I told him about the mangoes and the spill, and he just smiled and said, ‘Participant, sometimes things happen. The important thing is to learn from them.’

I tried walking to the market this morning, just for fifteen minutes. It was hard at first, my legs felt wobbly, but I kept going. I even bought an apple for my lunch! It tasted really good, sweeter than usual. Mr. Maphalane still wants that big order for the weekend, and I’m going to try to do it better this time. I’m taking breaks, drinking water, and remembering what Dr. Sithole said.  It’s not easy changing habits, but I feel a little bit stronger, a little bit better. Maybe, just maybe, I can do this. I can feel myself getting a little bit more energy, and I think I’m starting to understand how important it is to take care of myself, even when I'm busy.

input.story:
My name is Participant, and I work at the market down by the river. It’s a busy place, always full of people buying and selling. I sell spices – turmeric, ginger, all sorts of lovely smells. Most days, I grab a quick pap en rusvet brood from the spaza shop near my house. It's cheap, and it fills my tummy. It’s easy, you know? But sometimes, after a long day shouting about prices, my legs feel all wobbly, and my head feels a bit funny. Like I’m walking in slow motion. I just put it down to being tired, honestly. It’s a simple life, isn’t it? But I always feel a bit sluggish.

Yesterday, Mr. Nkosi asked me to help him sort the fresh vegetables for the big order he’s taking to the hotel. He said it was important, and he needed someone who could work quickly. I wanted to do a good job, so I agreed. But I was still feeling a bit off. I grabbed a banana and a biscuit – that’s what I always do when I’m busy. But halfway through, I just… slumped. I couldn’t lift the heavy boxes of tomatoes, and my hands were shaking. Mr. Nkosi looked really disappointed. He said, ‘Participant, you need to take care of yourself. You can’t work well if you’re not feeling okay.’ It made me feel a bit silly, but he was right, wasn’t he?

Dr. Khumalo at the clinic explained that the food I was eating – the pap and biscuits – they can make my blood sugar go up and down. She said it’s important to eat things that won’t do that, like fruits and vegetables, and maybe some chicken or fish. She gave me a little booklet with pictures of healthy food. It looked complicated, to be honest. I asked her, ‘But how can I afford all this fancy food when I’m just selling spices?’ She smiled and said, ‘Small changes, Participant. Start with one thing at a time.’ She also told me to check my sugar levels regularly. It all felt a bit overwhelming, but I promised to try.

I started small. Instead of a pap and biscuit, I grabbed an apple and a handful of nuts after my shift. It wasn’t as quick, but it felt… better. My legs didn’t feel so wobbly, and my head was clearer. Mr. Nkosi even noticed! He said, ‘Participant, you seem much brighter today. You’re working like a machine!’ And then, the big order came through – a huge delivery for the hotel. I sorted the vegetables with confidence, lifting the boxes easily. It wasn’t just about doing a good job; it was about feeling good while I did it. Now, I think I’ll even try adding some spinach to my meals. It’s a small step, but it feels like a big one. I'm feeling good, and that's what matters, isn't it?

input.question: I don't have a gym—what can I do at home or with everyday items to stay active?
input.story:
My name is Participant, and life here in [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] is…well, it’s work. Every day is about the goats, the little farm, making sure we have enough to sell at the market. I don’t think much about feeling tired, or what I eat. If there’s food, I eat it. Usually, that’s tuwo shinkafa with maybe some vegetable soup if my wife, Participant, has been to the market. Sometimes, late at night, after everyone is asleep, I have a little fura da nono – it’s sweet, and I like it. Today, I was supposed to repair the fence around the goat pen, a small job, really. But I just…couldn't get going. Felt heavy, sluggish. Kept sitting down, saying I'd start in a minute. The goats, they took their chance and wandered into old man Participant's yam field. That wasn’t good. He wasn't pleased.

Participant, she noticed I was dragging myself around. She insisted I go to the clinic in Wudil. I didn't want to, thought it was a waste of time. What would they tell me that I didn’t already know? But she was firm. The nurse, a kind woman named Participant, she spoke Hausa, thank goodness. She checked my blood sugar – high, she said. She explained, slowly, that the late-night snacks, even something small like fura, were messing with my sugar. She said if I wanted to have the strength to build a good, strong fence for the goats, and to be ready for the bigger work of preparing the field for the rainy season, I needed to eat more regularly during the day and avoid sugar at night. She said small changes, like swapping the fura for a handful of groundnuts before bed, could make a difference. It sounded…possible, I suppose.

Trying to change things is harder than it sounds. Old habits, you know? I still found myself craving something sweet after dinner. The first night, I gave in and had a little fura. The next day, I felt that same sluggishness. The goats seemed to sense it too, testing the weak spots in the fence. I had to rush to fix it before they caused more trouble. But I remembered Participant’s words about the field. Preparing that field is important. It’s the biggest job of the year, and if I’m not strong, we won’t have a good harvest. So, I forced myself to eat a handful of groundnuts instead. It wasn't the same, but it quieted the craving… a little.

It’s been a week now, and things are…better. I’m eating more tuwo and vegetables during the day, and Participant is helping me. We're even adding more moringa leaves to the soup – she says it’s good for everything! The late-night cravings are still there sometimes, but the groundnuts help. And I have more energy. I started working on the field yesterday, and I didn't feel as tired as I expected. I managed to clear a good patch before the sun got too high. Old man Participant even complimented me on the new, stronger fence. Maybe this health business isn’t so bad after all. I might even ask Participant about other ways to stay strong. It seems looking after myself isn't just for me, but for my goats, my family, and the harvest to come.

input.question: [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE]
input.story:
Wallahi, life as a [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] in [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] keeps a man busy. Every day is the same – wake up, pray, a quick bowl of tuwo shinkafa with miyan kuka for breakfast, rush to the office. Lunch is usually something small from a roadside vendor, maybe some suya and a drink. I like my food, you see? It’s what we grew up with. My wife tries to get me to eat more vegetables, but…well, a man needs his fill! Today, the head of department asked me to prepare a report on new land allocations. A small task, really. But I couldn't concentrate. My head was foggy, and my legs felt heavy. I kept rereading the same sentences, making silly mistakes. I just couldn’t get the numbers to add up right. I blamed it on the heat, but deep down, I knew something wasn’t quite right.

My friend, Malam Musa, noticed I wasn't myself. He’s a retired teacher and always tells me to take care of myself. He insisted I visit the clinic at the local government office. I was hesitant, you know? Doctors… always telling you what to do. But Musa was firm. At the clinic, the nurse, Sister Participant, was very kind. She listened patiently as I explained my tiredness and the trouble with the report. She checked my blood sugar, and her face became serious. 'Alhaji Participant,' she said, 'your sugar is high. You have diabetes. It’s affecting your energy and concentration. You need to watch your diet – less tuwo shinkafa, more vegetables, and a good walk every day. Even 30 minutes can make a difference.' She gave me a simple chart with pictures of healthy foods and a walking schedule. It didn't seem so bad when she explained it like that, and she assured me it wouldn't interfere with my prayers.

Trying to change a lifetime of habits is harder than it looks, I tell you! The first few days were tough. I missed my big bowl of tuwo shinkafa. My wife tried making me more vegetable-based soups, but it just didn’t feel satisfying. I tried to walk after work, but I was always too tired. One evening, I gave in and had a plate of fried akara with a sugary drink. The next day, I felt even worse. But then I remembered the bigger report, the one the head of department was waiting for. If I couldn't even manage a small task when I was feeling unwell, how would I handle something important? So, I forced myself to walk, even if it was just around the block, and I started swapping tuwo shinkafa for more beans and vegetables. It wasn't easy, but I kept reminding myself of the report.

Slowly, things started to improve. The headaches became less frequent, and I found I could concentrate for longer periods. The walking, surprisingly, started to feel good. I even started joining Malam Musa for his evening strolls. I finished the land allocation report, and the head of department was pleased. He even praised my attention to detail! It wasn’t just the report, though. I felt…lighter, more energetic. Sister Participant was happy when I went back for a check-up, and my blood sugar was down. She encouraged me to keep up the good work and suggested I join a community walking group. I’m still getting used to the changes, but I’m starting to realize that taking care of my health isn’t about denying myself pleasures, it’s about finding a balance. Maybe, just maybe, this is a good thing. I’m even thinking about trying to learn how to make a proper moringa salad from my wife. Who knows what else I might discover?

input.question: [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE]
input.story:
My name is Participant, and I'm a [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] here in [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE]. Every day is busy, busy, busy! I sell kola nuts at the market, you know, the ones people chew to stay awake and feel strong. I like to start my day with strong, sweet tea and maybe a puff of cigarette – gets me going, right? Then, it’s straight to the market. Today, I had a small order to fill for Alhaji Musa, just fifty kola nuts for a wedding. Easy work, I thought. But halfway through sorting them, I felt… *weak*. Like my legs were made of water. I had to sit down, and even then, my hands were shaking. I just couldn’t seem to focus, and I messed up the order, giving Alhaji Musa the wrong count. He wasn’t happy, not happy at all. I wondered, what was going on with me?

Old Mama Participant, the woman who sells dates next to my stall, saw me looking pale. She’s a wise woman, that one. She told me, 'Participant, you need to go see Doctor Participant at the clinic. You look like you're running on empty.' I didn’t want to go, honestly. Clinics are for sick people, and I'm a strong man! But Mama Participant insisted, saying, 'It’s not about being strong, it's about being *smart* strong.' So, I went. Doctor Participant checked me, asked about my tea and cigarettes, and told me about my sugar. He said it was too high, and that's why I was feeling weak. He didn't tell me to stop everything, just to be careful. 'Eat more things like beans and maize, Participant,' he said. 'They release sugar slowly. And maybe swap some of that sweet tea for water, eh?' It sounded… doable. I could try, couldn't I?

Trying to change things is hard, I tell you! The first day, I tried to have beans with my tea. It just didn't taste right! I missed the sweetness. And the cigarette… oh, the cigarette called to me all morning. I almost gave in, but then I remembered Alhaji Musa's wedding. I had a bigger order coming up – two hundred kola nuts for a naming ceremony. If I messed *that* up, my reputation would be ruined. So, I forced myself to eat the beans, even though my face was making funny shapes. I drank water with my tea, and it felt… bland. But I kept at it. It was tough, really tough, but I told myself, 'Just for the naming ceremony, Participant. Just until you finish the work.'

Slowly, slowly, things started to get better. The beans didn't taste so bad after a few days. I even started adding a little pepper to them, like Mama Participant does. And I cut back on the cigarettes, having only one or two instead of a pack. I still had my sweet tea, but I drank less of it. When the day of the naming ceremony came, I felt… different. I wasn't shaky, and my head was clear. I sorted those two hundred kola nuts quickly and accurately, and the family was very pleased. Alhaji Participant, the father of the new baby, even gave me a generous tip! After that, I started thinking, maybe Doctor Participant was right. Maybe eating better and cutting back on the cigarettes isn't just about the work, it’s about feeling good *all* the time. Maybe, just maybe, I should learn more about what I can eat to stay strong, for a long time.

input.question: Eating healthy can get expensive—how can I manage a nutritious diet on a tight budget? And can I still enjoy some traditional foods?
input.story:
Hai, my name is Participant, and life as a [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] in [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] market is…busy, wallahi! Every day is a hustle. I sell beautiful fabrics, Ankara and lace, you know? Bright colours, good quality. But let me tell you, thinking about what to eat is always last on my mind. Usually, it’s whatever’s quickest – maybe some masa with a little stew, or tuwo shinkafa with miyan kuka. Sometimes, if I’m lucky, some grilled fish. It fills the belly, right? Just last week, I had a big order to prepare - a wedding set! I promised the customer it would be ready on Wednesday. But I felt so tired, so sluggish, I kept making mistakes with the measurements. I had to redo a whole piece of lace! Honestly, I just thought it was stress. What does eating have to do with sewing, anyway?

My friend, Participant, she noticed I wasn’t myself. She said I looked tired and worried about my work. She practically dragged me to the local clinic. The nurse, a kind woman named Hauwa, listened to me complain about the tiredness and the messed-up wedding order. She didn’t laugh when I said I didn’t see what food had to do with it! Hauwa explained about the sugar in my blood, about diabetes, and how it can make you feel weak and affect your concentration. She said I need to eat more vegetables, more beans, and less of the sugary things. 'Participant,' she said, 'you can still enjoy your masa and tuwo, but maybe with a bigger portion of vegetables and a smaller portion of the stew. And try to walk for at least thirty minutes most days.' It sounded…hard. But then I remembered that big order for Alhaji Participant's daughter. I *had* to get it right this time.

Trying to change things was…difficult, I won’t lie. I’m used to a certain way of eating, you see? The first day, I tried to make a big plate of vegetables with my tuwo. My neighbour, Auntie Participant, came over for tea and she looked at my plate like I was eating grass! 'Participant, are you alright?' she asked, worried. I almost gave up and went back to my usual portion of stew. But then I thought about the beautiful silk Alhaji Participant wanted, and how much money I would make if I didn't mess it up. So, I kept eating my vegetables, even though it felt strange. And the walking? My feet were aching! But I walked to the market and back, slowly, slowly. It wasn't easy, but I told myself, 'Just for the work, Participant, just for the work.'

Slowly, things started to change. I started adding more okra and spinach to my soups, and I swapped white rice for brown rice sometimes. I even started enjoying it! The tiredness wasn't as bad, and I could concentrate on my sewing for longer. When I finally finished Alhaji Participant’s wedding set, it was perfect, wallahi! Every stitch was neat, every piece of lace was measured exactly right. He was so pleased, he gave me a generous tip. And you know what? I felt proud, not just of the money, but of myself. Hauwa was right. Eating better really did help. Now, I'm thinking maybe I should try to walk a little faster, and maybe even add some fruit to my breakfast. It seems like taking care of myself isn't just about feeling good, it’s about being able to do everything I want to do, and do it well.

input.story:
Ag, man, life is busy, you know? I'm Participant, and I sell spices down at the market in Johannesburg. Good spices, mind you! But these days, just walking to the shop feels… heavy. I start my day with a strong, sweet tea and a vetkoek with polony, gotta have something quick. Yesterday, Old Man Themba asked me to deliver a big bag of chilli powder to his shop across town. Just a little walk, I thought. But halfway there, I was sweating like a pig, my chest tight, and I had to stop three times to catch my breath. I left the chilli powder with a neighbour and promised Themba I’d bring it later. Honestly, I just felt… tired. Like someone switched off the lights a little bit inside me. Is this just getting old, or what?

My wife, Participant, she saw me struggling. She’s a smart woman, Participant. She took me to the clinic down the road. Sister Nomusa, she’s a good nurse, always smiling. She checked my blood sugar and said it was a bit high. 'Participant,' she said, 'you need to move your body more, and maybe watch the sweet things a little.' I told her, 'But Sister, I *work* all day! And a man needs his tea!' She just chuckled and said, 'Even a little walk each day, maybe 30 minutes, can make a big difference. Start small. And try swapping the polony for some beans sometimes, hey?' It sounded… doable, I guess. But thirty minutes? Every day? That's a long time!

Okay, so I tried. First day, I walked around the block after work. Thirty minutes felt like thirty years! My legs were burning, and I kept wanting to stop for a cool drink. I even forgot to walk with Themba’s chilli powder! He gave me a proper telling-off, he did. But I remembered the big order coming up – a restaurant wanted a whole crate of my special Durban curry blend. It’s a big deal, a lot of money. I couldn't be puffing and panting trying to carry it. So, I tried again the next day. Shorter walk, slower pace. I even managed to walk with the chilli powder to Themba's shop this time. It was still hard, but a little bit easier. A little…hopeful.

After a week, something strange started happening. The walks weren’t so bad anymore. I started feeling… lighter. I even started adding a few extra minutes each day. I swapped the polony for baked beans most mornings, and Participant started making me more salads with dinner. When the day came to deliver the curry blend, I didn’t even break a sweat! I carried the crate all the way to the restaurant, chatting with the chef like it was nothing. He was so impressed, he ordered another one for next week! I felt proud, strong. Sister Nomusa was right. Maybe this health thing isn't so bad after all. Maybe I'll even try a little jog next week. What do you think?

input.question: [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE]
input.story:
Hayi bo, life, isn't it something? I'm Participant, and I’m a carpenter, a good one if I do say so myself. I build those lovely wooden window frames you see in the newer houses around here in Soweto. But lately, things haven't been so smooth. I always start my day with a nice strong cup of tea and a vetkoek from Mama Rose's stall – they're just so good, you know? Then I work, work, work. But I find myself getting tired quickly these days. Just last week, I promised old Mr. Dlamini I'd fix his kitchen cupboard door by Friday. I thought, easy peasy! But by Thursday evening, I was so sleepy, I just couldn't focus. Ended up leaving it unfinished. Mr. Dlamini wasn't happy, and honestly, I wasn't either. I just kept thinking, what’s happening to me?

My wife, Participant, she saw I was worried. She took me to the clinic, you know, the one near the taxi rank. The sister, she was very kind. She checked my sugar levels and said, 'Participant, you have diabetes, and it looks like you're eating too much sugar, especially late at night.' I was a bit surprised, to be honest. I didn’t think late-night snacks were such a big deal! She explained that when I eat sweet things before bed, my body struggles to deal with the sugar while I'm sleeping, and that makes me tired. She told me to try and have a small plate of pap and some fish instead of those koeksisters I love. She said, 'It won't be easy, but it will help you feel stronger and work better.' I thought, pap and fish? Instead of something sweet? It sounded…difficult.

Okay, so I tried the pap and fish. First night, I was dreaming about those koeksisters, I tell you! It was hard, really hard. I even sneaked a small piece of chocolate one evening, thinking, 'Just one won't hurt.' But the next day, I felt sluggish again. And I had a big job coming up – building a whole set of doors for a new house in Diepkloof. It was a good job, a lot of money, and I *needed* to be at my best. That's what kept me going. I reminded myself that if I wanted to finish those doors properly, I had to stick to the sister’s advice. I started having a small glass of milk with my pap too, Participant suggested it. It helped a little.

Slowly, things started to change. The tiredness wasn't as bad. I found myself waking up feeling a bit more rested. I still missed my late-night sweets, but I started finding other things to enjoy – a nice cup of rooibos tea, for example. And those doors in Diepkloof? I finished them on time, and Mr. Nkosi, the owner, was very pleased! He even gave me a bonus. I felt so proud, not just of the doors, but of myself. I realised that taking care of my health wasn't just about avoiding sickness, it was about being able to do the things I love, and provide for my family. Maybe, just maybe, this healthy eating thing isn’t so bad after all. I'm even thinking about asking the sister for some tips on getting more exercise. What do you know, maybe I can even start running again!

As a [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] in suburban [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE], my day starts early. I wake up before dawn to pray and then head to the market to buy fresh produce. I've been doing this for years, but lately, I've been feeling tired easily. I think it's because I'm not eating well. I often skip breakfast and rely on sugary snacks to get me through the day. My friends tell me I need to eat more vegetables and fruits, but I'm not sure what to do. I've tried a few times to change my diet, but it's hard to stick to it. I want to be healthy, but I don't know where to start. My biggest task is to manage my hypertension, and I'm not sure how to do it without giving up my favorite foods.

One day, I went to see a health worker at the local clinic. She asked me about my diet and lifestyle, and I told her about my struggles. She also encouraged me to take a short walk each day to help reduce stress.

I decided to give it a try. I started by adding some fruits and vegetables to my meals and cutting back on sugary snacks. It wasn't easy at first, but I persisted. I also started taking short walks around the market during my breaks. I felt a bit silly at first, but it actually helped me clear my head and feel more energized. I started to notice improvements in my overall health, and it motivated me to keep going.

It's been a few months now, and I've seen significant improvements in my health. My blood pressure has decreased, and I have more energy throughout the day. I've also lost a bit of weight, which has boosted my confidence. I've learned to make healthy choices and stick to them. I'm now open to learning more about nutrition and making adjustments to my diet as needed. I'm grateful for the guidance I received from the health worker, and I'm excited to see where this new journey takes me.

input.question: I don't have a gym—what can I do at home or with everyday items to stay active?
input.story:
As a young [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE], I wake up early, feeling a mix of excitement and stress. Today is a big day; I have orders to fulfill for customers across the city. I quickly get dressed in my worn but comfortable clothes and rush out the door to start my day. My diet consists mainly of street food and whatever I can afford at the local market. I've never really thought much about what I eat or how it affects my body, as long as I feel okay. My daily routine is hectic, and I often skip meals or grab whatever is readily available, which can be high in sugar and unhealthy fats. I've always been active, but with the demands of my work, I've noticed my energy levels dropping, and I've started to feel a bit more sluggish than usual. I try to push through, but it's getting harder. I need a way to manage my energy levels and stay focused throughout the day.

I decided to visit the local health clinic to see if they could offer any advice on how to improve my health. The nurse practitioner there was kind and listened attentively to my concerns. She explained that my diet and lack of exercise were contributing to my fatigue and suggested a few simple changes I could make to my daily routine. I was skeptical at first, but she assured me that these changes would make a big difference in how I felt. She recommended that I start by eating smaller, more frequent meals throughout the day, including plenty of fruits and vegetables. She also suggested that I try to incorporate some light exercise, like walking or yoga, into my daily routine. I was hesitant to make these changes, but she encouraged me to give it a try.

I tried to implement the nurse practitioner's suggestions, but it wasn't easy. I found it hard to adjust to eating smaller meals throughout the day, and I missed the rush of energy I used to get from grabbing a quick snack or meal. I also struggled to find the time to exercise, especially with my busy schedule. But I was determined to make this work, not just for my health but also because I had a bigger goal in mind - to start my own business and become financially independent. I knew that if I could just get my health under control, I'd be better equipped to handle the demands of entrepreneurship. So, I persisted, even when it felt like giving up. I started small, taking short walks during my breaks or doing a few yoga poses in the morning. It wasn't much, but it was a start.

As the days went by, I started to notice a difference in how I felt. My energy levels were higher, and I was able to focus better throughout the day. I still had my busy moments, but I was better equipped to handle them. I realized that taking care of my health wasn't just about feeling good; it was also about being more productive and successful in my work. With my newfound energy and focus, I was able to tackle my bigger goal - starting my own business. It wasn't easy, but I was determined to make it happen. And as I looked back on the journey, I realized that taking care of my health had been the key to unlocking my potential. I was no longer just a young [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE]; I was a [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE], ready to take on the world.

I became more open to learning about healthy habits and was motivated to continue making positive changes to my lifestyle.

input.question: I don't have a gym—what can I do at home or with everyday items to stay active?
input.story:
I wake up every morning, get ready for work on my farm, and head out to tend to my crops. As a [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE], I need to be physically fit to keep up with the demands of my job. But to be honest, I haven't been taking care of my health like I should. I love playing football with my friends, but I haven't been able to join them as much as I used to. My diet consists of mostly traditional Hausa dishes like tuwo and miyan kubewa, which are delicious but not always the healthiest. I've been having some issues with my blood sugar levels, and my doctor has been reminding me to take my [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] regularly. But I often find myself neglecting my health needs, and it shows in my work. Just the other day, I was trying to fix a broken fence on my farm, but I ended up getting tired easily and had to leave it for another day.

I decided to visit my local healthcare clinic to get some advice on how to manage my health better. The healthcare worker, Sister Participant, was very kind and understanding. She explained to me that as a person with type 2 diabetes, I need to be mindful of my diet and physical activity. She advised me to start with small, achievable goals, like taking a 30-minute walk every day and eating more fruits and vegetables. She also reminded me to take my [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] on time and to monitor my blood sugar levels regularly. I was a bit resistant at first, but she reassured me that it's never too late to make a change.

I tried to follow Sister Participant's advice, but it wasn't easy. I had to adjust my routine to fit in the daily walks and healthy meals. There were times when I felt like giving up, especially when I had to sacrifice my favorite foods. But I kept reminding myself of the upcoming harvest season, when I'll need to be in top shape to work long hours on my farm. I persisted, and slowly but surely, I started to notice improvements in my energy levels and overall health. However, I did have a minor setback when I forgot to take my insulin injection one morning, and I had to deal with the consequences.

It's been a few weeks since I started making changes to my lifestyle, and I can already see the difference. I'm able to work longer hours on my farm without getting tired, and I've even started playing football with my friends again. I feel more confident and in control of my health. The harvest season is approaching, and I'm excited to tackle the challenges that come with it. I'm grateful for Sister Participant's guidance and support, and I'm open to continuing to learn and improve my health habits. Who knows, maybe one day I'll even start a football team for farmers in my community!

As I look back on my journey, I realize that taking care of my health is not just about me, but about my community and my livelihood. As a [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE], I need to be physically fit to provide for my family and contribute to my community. I'm proud of the progress I've made, and I'm excited to see where this new path takes me. I know that I'll face challenges along the way, but I'm ready to take them on, one step at a time. And who knows, maybe one day I'll be able to share my story with others and inspire them to take control of their health too.

input.question: I don't have a gym—what can I do at home or with everyday items to stay active?
input.story:
Let me tell you how my normal day goes, eh? Every morning, I wake up just before sunrise, say my prayers, and get ready for the market. Sometimes my breakfast is just a small plate of tuwo shinkafa and left-over miyan kuka from last night—quick and filling, sha. By the time I finish sweeping my small flat, sorting out my fabrics, and rushing to the stall, I’m already tired before customers even start coming. The other day, I wanted to rearrange my stock shelves and make the table neat—simple task, bah? But by halfway, my head was spinning, my hands shaky, and I had to sit down. I just told myself, ‘Ah, maybe it’s the sun or small tiredness, it will pass.’ But deep down, I wondered, 'Is it not just me being lazy?' 

After that, I dragged myself to the clinic since my medication was almost finished. Nurse Halima saw me looking drained, and instead of shouting, she sat beside me. She asked, ‘Participant, do you move your body at all when you’re not trading?’ I laughed, ‘Me, gym? Where do I get time for running around after work, eh?’ She smiled and shook her head, ‘You don’t need a gym, my sister. Just start with what you have—walk around your room, dance while you sweep, stretch your arms after every two customers. Even prayers add movement. Try and do these small things, then next week see if you feel better. Body like machine—it needs to move, even if it’s little.’ Her advice sounded easy but strange. Still, it’s from nurse, so maybe I should try.

The next morning, I started by stretching my arms before I got out of bed. Uhm—honestly, that one was not easy; everything stiff, as if my joints refused. I tried walking up and down my small passage after sweeping. My legs screamed, 'Why now?' and my mind fought, wanting to just rest before work started. But then I remembered—next week, I have to re-stock all my fabrics at Dawanu market, a big job needing strength. I sighed and told myself, ‘Participant, even if it’s small, just do it, so you don’t disgrace yourself for market front.’ I counted my steps as motivation, even though sweat soaked my hijab under the hot room.

Kai, see as days passed, eh! My body slowly got used to the stretching and short walks. I started feeling less tired at the stall and, wallahi, didn’t rush to sit down so quickly. When Dawanu Market day finally came, I lifted my fabric bales with more ease and didn’t beg for help, even from the big men. It shocked me, y’know? Maybe small movement is not just wahala. Now, I think I could even try more—maybe some dancing in the kitchen while waiting for my moi moi to finish. Step by step, my confidence came back. I’m not there fully, but at least I know my health does small magic if I just listen and try every day.

input.question: [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE]
input.story:
Every day for me, Participant, is early rising and rushing to the Sabon Gari market, hoping today’s trade will go well. Wallahi, as a [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] in [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE], you know the bustle does not wait for anybody. Sometimes, work makes me eat late—maybe tuwo shinkafa with a quick splash of soup after I close, tired and thinking, ‘If I miss food, how will I get the strength for tomorrow?’ I remember one night last week, I stayed till late counting my money, ate my heavy food close to midnight, and drifted off to sleep. The next morning, my body was heavy, my head spun, and my sugar shot up. I couldn’t open my stall in time and lost some early customers. Can you imagine how just one meal at the wrong time can spoil business?

Not long after, at the health clinic near my mosque, I met Nurse Participant during my insulin refill. She asked about my meal times, and I laughed it off, ‘Business is busy, nurse, man must hustle!’ She shook her head, ‘Participant, late eating can push your blood sugar up overnight and make you weak. Try to eat your main meal by Maghrib, two hours before sleep, and keep some fruit or water if hunger comes late. This will help your insulin work and give you energy for trading. You want to win at the next big Sallah market, ba?’ Her advice was simple, like advice from a big sister I wish I had listened to earlier.

That night, I did my best to close shop early. The smell of masa at the roadside tempted me, but I reached home and ate rice and fresh ugu stew before the call for Isha prayer. The first days were not easy. Sometimes I felt hunger while packing up goods or watching football highlights at home. One time, I almost grabbed a late suya stick, but then I remembered I still had a larger order to supply next week—how will I do that if I am sick now? I forced myself to try fruits or just drink water if night hunger talked too much.

Two weeks later, I felt lighter when waking up, and my mornings carried less dizziness. That big order from the electronics dealer came, and, walahi, I finished it without missing a customer. My sugar stayed steady, and I found I could join my friends for an early football game on the weekend. Seeing how these small changes made my big work go easier, I now want to learn even more ways to keep strong and healthy. Maybe good health, like good trade, grows bit by bit if you do the right thing every day.

input.question: [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE]
input.story:
Every morning I wake up early, before the call to prayer, and I walk among the green rice fields. I always pack my lunch in a simple plastic bowl, sometimes it is rice, sometimes bread spread with margarine. I never really thought much about how my food affects how I move or work. One day, I tried to clear the small canal for water in my own field. You ever feel so weak in your arms even though you lift things every day? My legs nearly gave way, and the spade dropped. I just sat down, sweating and breathing fast. Why can't I even finish this small job?

Later, I had to go for my normal checkup at the clinic in town. The nurse, Participant, she asked what I ate that day. I told her about my rice and my bread. She shook her head gently, not angry, just concerned. She explained, 'Participant, for your diabetes, some foods like white rice and bread can make your blood sugar go high fast. Try more brown rice, beans, vegetables, grilled fish. Add fresh fruit, like guava or orange, not the sweet drinks. And never skip your food, even when you are busy on the farm.' I laughed softly. Why must it sound so easy when my body wants old habits?

input.question: Sometimes I feel tired or discouraged—how can I stay motivated, [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE]
input.story:
Every morning, I wake up in my small house in the suburbs of [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE], thinking about my business. I run a small shop near the main road, selling fabrics and household things. Most days, I stand behind my counter and work long hours without much movement. Sometimes, I just grab a quick rice and stew lunch from the pot, not really thinking about what my body needs. Last week, I tried to rearrange my shelves for a new stock arrival. But halfway, tiredness hit me, and my hands started shaking a bit. I could not finish that task. I just sat there, confused, wondering if it is from my sugar or maybe I am just not strong like before.

Later, I went to the local clinic nearby for my yearly check-up. The nurse, Mrs. Esther, looked at me and asked, 'How do you feel these days, Participant?' I told her honestly, 'A bit tired, and I’m just not sure what I’m doing wrong.' She smiled kindly and said, 'You know, a little walking every day—even around your shop—will help your sugar and give you more strength. It does not need to be hard. Just 10 or 15 minutes in the morning, then again in the evening. Can you try?' I was not sure at first—it sounded too simple. But something about her gentle way made me nod.

So, the next day, I took her advice and tried to walk around my shop’s grounds in the morning before opening. Eh, my feet felt so heavy! I walked in my simple slippers, feeling awkward, wondering if my neighbours were watching. I almost gave up. But then, I remembered I had a big stock delivery coming next week, and if small tasks made me weak, how could I handle bigger ones? I took a deep breath, wiped sweat from my forehead, and promised myself to try each day.

Days passed, and I noticed small changes. My legs felt less tired, and I did not need to sit as much during the day. When the big delivery truck came, I surprised myself. I moved boxes with energy I thought I had lost. As I wiped my hands and looked at my arranged shelves, I smiled and thought, 'Maybe, little by little, exercise really helps.' Now, I feel ready to keep going, one day at a time, stronger for my shop and myself.

input.story:
My name is Participant and I always thought walking around my kasi in Johannesburg was enough to keep me healthy. After all, I buy fresh tomatoes and spinach from the spaza down the road, and sometimes I help carry heavy water buckets for Gogo. The other day, though, when my boss asked me to carry a big box of files to the upstairs office, I struggled to get up without stopping to catch my breath. Hey, isn’t walking everywhere enough? Clearly, I was missing something.

Later that week, I popped into the clinic where Nurse Lerato, with her bright green uniform, called me aside. She smiled and shook her head when I told her about my ‘exercise programme’. She said, 'Participant, walking is a great start, but your body needs different moves to stay strong. Do a bit of stretching, try lifting small things, or even join us for aerobics outside the centre on Wednesdays. It doesn’t have to be fancy. You can start small, neh?' I nodded, not sure if I was ready, but Nurse Lerato always talks sense.

Back home, I tried stretching before my evening walk to the local shop, but I felt stiff and a bit silly. One uncle passing by laughed and asked if I was training for Comrades marathon! For a moment, I wanted to give up and just stick to my usual route. But, remembering that next week I had to help set up big chairs for our neighbour’s wedding, I kept going. Maybe a little bit of stretching wouldn’t hurt, right?

After a few days, I started noticing my legs felt less heavy and climbing stairs wasn’t such a mission anymore. On Saturday, when it was time to arrange all those chairs at the wedding hall, I finished the job without huffing and puffing. My friends even teased, 'Participant, you look fresh today!' Eish, who knew a bit of extra exercise could help like this? Now, I actually listen out for new tips. Next time, maybe I’ll try those aerobics on Wednesday!

input.question: Sometimes I feel tired or discouraged—how can I stay motivated, [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE]
input.story:
Hello, my name is Participant, and let me tell you, being a [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] in the busy city can make you forget about your own health! Every morning, I like to eat white bread with jam and quickly rush out to open my little shop. The city never waits for anyone, you know? Last Tuesday, I had a pile of receipts to check, a small but important task before the big monthly report. But what happened? By ten in the morning I felt so tired and a bit dizzy, I mixed up all the numbers and had to start over. I even wondered, 'How come something so simple was so difficult today?'

Later that day, I decided to visit the local clinic nearby for a check-up. The nurse greeted me with a warm smile and said, 'Participant, maybe your food choices are making your blood sugar go up and down.' At first, I laughed and said, 'But I don’t eat sweets all the time!' The nurse patiently explained, 'It’s not just sweets—try to swap white bread for whole grain, add more vegetables, and walk a bit each day. These small changes help your body keep energy steady, so you don’t feel so tired at work.' Her advice sounded simple, but could I really do it every day?

The next morning, I tried making brown bread with avocado and took a short walk before opening my shop. I felt a bit silly walking around the block and missed my fast breakfast. At lunchtime, I nearly grabbed my normal fizzy drink, but I remembered the nurse’s words. Still, I felt grumpy and nearly gave up—old habits can be tough to break, hey! But I kept reminding myself of the big monthly report I needed to finish well this time. That made me push through the day with the healthier choices.

Day by day, I started feeling less tired in the mornings, and I noticed fewer mistakes in my work. When the big monthly report came, I finished it with a clear head and even impressed my business partner with my neat records. Could you believe it, I felt proud of myself for trying new foods and a bit of exercise! Now, I’m not scared to keep learning new things for my health—maybe next week I’ll even try a dance class for fun!

input.question: I don't have a gym—what can I do at home or with everyday items to stay active?
input.story:
You know, every day starts early for me, setting up my little stall in the busy [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] market. I eat quick meals, often whatever's handy — sometimes leftover tuwo shinkafa and maybe a little soup. But I never really thought about how what I eat or how I move during my day might affect my sugar levels or energy. One afternoon, I tried to stay longer at the market to sell more, but I got tired so fast, and my sugar felt all over the place. I reckoned maybe I just need to push through, but after that day, I knew something was off. How else am I to keep up with my customers if I’m running out of steam?

So, I went to the local health clinic, and a nurse there explained things differently. She told me it wasn’t about pushing harder but about working smarter with my body. She suggested simple exercises I could do at home using everyday items, like carrying water jugs or stretching while watching my children play. She also talked about adjusting my meals, like adding some moringa leaves or eating beans more often — foods I already know and trust from back home but cooked a bit differently. I was a bit sceptical, thinking, 'How can small moves and simple foods really make a difference?' But she made it sound doable without fancy gyms or expensive foods.

I tried those exercises the next morning, but oh boy, my muscles were tight, and I almost gave up after a few stretches. It isn't easy changing long habits, especially when the market calls early and I must be alert. I also found myself craving the usual heavy meals instead of the lighter ones the nurse mentioned. One day, I even skipped the exercises because I was too tired. Still, with a small event coming up where I had to manage a bigger order of goods at the market, I didn’t want to lose face or energy. So I kept telling myself, 'Just one more day, I can handle this.'

Slowly, things began to click. I started walking around the stall more, stretching my arms and legs between customers, and packing small packets of beans or miyan kuka with extra veggies to eat during breaks. I wasn’t perfect, but I felt less drained by midday. The day I managed the big order, I was surprised at how much more confident and sharper I felt, even after hours on my feet. Now, I see how keeping active and eating right, even just a little differently, helps me run my business better. I’m starting to think maybe this health journey isn’t such a bother after all — who knows what I can do next?

input.question: I don't have a gym—what can I do at home or with everyday items to stay active?
input.story:
You know, sometimes I get caught up in my trading, selling fabrics in the busy market here in [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE]. I just assume moving around the stalls and talking to customers is enough exercise for me. But honestly, I never really thought about how important it is to keep active in a focused way for my diabetes. One day, I tried to manage everything without any real plan, believing I could just walk a bit when I had time. But when I felt tired and my sugar was high, work just didn’t go well. My customers noticed I was off, and I wasn’t my sharp self. Who knew a little exercise done right would make such a difference?

Then I went to the local health clinic where the nurse explained things clearly in Hausa, just like talking to a friend. She said walking briskly for at least 30 minutes five times a week is perfect and showed me some simple exercises I can do at home, like using water bottles as weights or stretching after prayer times. She reminded me these are ways I can keep modest and still be active, even without a gym. I was a bit unsure at first, wondering if I could fit this into my busy routine, but she encouraged me to start small and be consistent, and always keep my sugar snacks handy just in case.

I tried to follow her advice the very next week. I started walking in the morning before the market opened, carrying empty jerry cans to do some lifting exercises in my compound, and stretching after reading Qur’an. But it wasn’t easy. Some days I felt lazy or worried about preparing for the market or study. One morning, I skipped my walk and felt sluggish all day. But I reminded myself of the big [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] event coming soon—a chance to show my best self—and that pushed me to keep going. It wasn’t perfect, but I knew my health mattered for this bigger goal.

Little by little, things got better. I felt stronger walking around the market and had more energy in my [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] groups. At the big [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] event, I was more confident than before and even shared some exercise tips with my friends. Now I understand that staying active with simple steps helps me control my diabetes better and keeps my life balanced. I’m even planning to start a small walking group with other women from my mosque. Who would have thought, just a few changes at home could open the door to a healthier and happier me?
